prompt.context: Your client is Next Level Gaming (NLG), a start-up in the E-sports and computer gaming industry based in Los Angeles, California. NLG is planning to launch its first game – an online, multiplayer role playing game that is unlike any existing franchise. Being a new player in the industry, NLG's CEO, Bobby Beck, has asked for your help in deciding its business model.
prompt.question: The company is considering 3 alternatives: a subscription model where players pay a monthly fee; a retail model where players pay full price at initial purchase; and a free-to-play model where the game is free to play but charges players for in-game merchandise. How would you advise NLG to proceed?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for this decision?
clarifying_info.a: NLG is looking to launch immediately.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the major competitors in the online gaming industry?
clarifying_info.a: The industry is dominated by 3 major players who control 35%, 25%, and 20% share respectively. There is a long tail of smaller gaming companies.
Based on preliminary market research, NLG expects the majority of players to be between the ages of 21 to 40.
NLG is planning to launch its game in the US only.

clarifying_info.q: What platforms will the game support?
clarifying_info.a: NLG's game is compatible for both Apple and Windows computers.

clarifying_info.q: What were the R&D costs to develop the game?
clarifying_info.a: NLG spent $10 million USD to develop its first game.

exhibits.title: Predicted Revenues
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three business models (Subscription, Retail, Free-To-Play) across revenue-related metrics

exhibits.title: Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: A table comparing per-customer and fixed costs across the three business models, with a footnote about free-to-play costs

data.Footnote: Per customer costs in the table are for all customers, including non-paying customers. Paying customers incur an additional average variable cost of $10

exhibits.title: Survey Info From Beta Test (n=100)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing average survey responses (scale 1–5) from beta test participants across four questions, broken out by the three business models

Questions: Continue playing this game after first year?
Purchase add-ons to the base game?
Switch to a new game in the same genre?
data.Note: 5 = most likely, 1 = least likely; a higher value is unfavorable for the last question (switching to competitor)

framework: Break down profitability for each of the 3 business models: revenue = # players acquired x $ revenue per player; costs = variable (per-player) costs + fixed costs
Estimate addressable market size (# of target players in the US) as a starting point for all three models
Calculate first-year revenues, costs, and profit (and margin) for each model using the exhibit data
Assess qualitative factors: competitive response risk, customer acquisition cost, player retention and loyalty, growth potential (new platforms, geographies, games), alternate revenue streams
Synthesize quantitative and qualitative findings into a recommendation with risks and mitigation

questions.prompt: What factors would you consider to estimate the number of players NLG can target with its first game? How large is this player base in the US?
questions.guidance: Candidate should scope to US online gamers aged 21–40 on PC (Apple or Windows). A reasonable top-down approach: US population ~330M, share aged 21–40 ~27% (~89M), share who are gamers ~30–35% (~27–31M), share on PC ~35–40% (~10M). Target addressable market is approximately 10 million players. Good answers may differ but should land near 10M; if significantly different, the interviewer should prompt the candidate to pressure-test assumptions.

math.setup: US population x % aged 21-40 x % who are gamers x % on PC
steps: 29M x ~35% PC share = ~10M PC gamers aged 21-40

questions.prompt: What is NLG's expected first-year profitability with each of the 3 pricing models? (Use Exhibits 1 and 2)
questions.guidance: Candidate must read Exhibit 1 for revenue drivers and Exhibit 2 for cost drivers. The key footnote in Exhibit 2 is critical: per-customer variable costs apply to ALL customers (including free non-paying ones), and paying customers in free-to-play incur an additional $10 variable cost. Strong candidates will calculate both absolute profit and profit margin. Candidate should note that subscription and free-to-play yield identical absolute profit ($20M) but at different margins, and retail is the least profitable on both measures.

math.setup: Revenue = target audience x market share x revenue per player; Costs = (players acquired x per-player variable + CAC) + fixed costs; Fixed costs = Product Dev + Server + Other = $5M + $7M + $3M = $15M
steps: Revenue: 10M x 10% x ($10/mo x 12 mo) = 1M x $120 = $120M
Variable + CAC costs (all 5M players): 5M x ($13 + $7) = 5M x $20 = $100M
Additional variable cost for paying players (5M x 30%): 1.5M x $10 = $15M
math.answer: Subscription: $20M profit (16.67% margin) | Retail: $9M profit (12.50% margin) | Free-to-Play: $20M profit (13.33% margin)

questions.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in choosing between the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate structures brainstorm into MECE buckets. Key considerations: (1) Competitive response — how sticky is the player base if a competitor launches in the same genre; free-to-play's larger base provides a buffer. (2) Growth potential — new platforms (mobile/console), new geographies, launching a 2nd generation game. (3) Alternate revenue streams — merchandising, hosting or participating in E-sports tournaments (requires sufficient player base). (4) Consumer preference shifts — migration to mobile, generational taste changes in game genre.

questions.prompt: How does the beta test survey data impact your outlook on the 3 different business models? [Exhibit 3 shown]
questions.guidance: Candidate should interpret all four survey questions. A higher score is favorable for questions 1–3 (retention, add-on purchases, referrals) and unfavorable for question 4 (switching to a competitor). Key insights: Retail model shows low intent to continue playing and low add-on purchase intent — low retention and low recurring revenue potential. Subscription and free-to-play both show high player loyalty (high scores on Q1–Q3). Free-to-play shows the lowest score on Q4 (least likely to switch), indicating the strongest competitive stickiness. Candidate should also note the sample size (n=100) is statistically significant.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in choosing between the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: How sticky is the player base if a competitor launches in the same genre?
Free-to-play's larger installed base (50% share vs. 10%) provides a stronger defensive moat
Subscription players may churn quickly if an alternative game launches

categories.name: Growth Potential
ideas: New platform expansion: from PC to mobile or console
New geography: expand outside of US
New game: launch a 2nd generation game to create new content and retain players
E-sports tournaments: contingent on reaching a sufficiently large player base

categories.name: Alternate Revenue Streams
ideas: E-sports tournament hosting or sponsorship revenue

categories.name: Consumer Preference Changes
ideas: Migration to mobile gaming platforms could erode PC player base
Generational shifts may cause new players to lose interest in current game genre
Subscription fatigue — consumers may resist adding another subscription service

recommendation: Recommend the free-to-play business model. It captures the largest player base (50% market share, 5M players) which provides the strongest competitive positioning and long-term growth optionality.

Although short-term profit is identical to subscription ($20M), free-to-play has greater upside through expanding the paying-player percentage, increasing in-game purchase revenue, and leveraging the large user base for E-sports and expansion to new platforms and geographies.
The beta test survey supports this: free-to-play players show the strongest loyalty and the lowest intent to switch to a competitor.
risks: Generating a sufficient percentage of paying players (currently assumed at 30%) is uncertain and critical to revenue
Revenue per paying player could be lower than the $100 annual estimate if in-game content is not compelling enough
Subscription model has a higher profit margin (16.67% vs. 13.33%) and more predictable revenue; if NLG prioritizes margin stability, subscription is defensible
next_steps: Design two distinct in-game purchase tiers: aesthetic upgrades (character customization) and time-saving upgrades (level progression) to maximize willingness-to-pay across different player segments
Conduct further market research to validate the 30% paying-player conversion assumption
Develop a roadmap for platform expansion (mobile/console) and geographic expansion to grow the addressable market
Explore E-sports tournament partnerships to build brand awareness and grow the player base
